fetched_contents.text: 4 Year Well-Child Checkup What Happens at the Visit? Your doctor and/or nurse will probably: 1. Check your child's weight and height, calculate body mass index (BMI), and plot the measurements on a growth chart. 2. Check your child's blood pressure, vision, and hearing using standard testing equipment. 3. Ask questions, address concerns, and offer advice about how your child is: Eating. Schedule three meals and two healthy snacks a day. If you have a picky eater, keep offering a variety of healthy foods for your child to choose from. Kids should be encouraged to give new foods a try, but don't force them to eat them. Peeing and pooping. By 4 years old, most kids are using the toilet. But many preschoolers who are potty trained during the day are not able to stay dry all night. It's also common for busy preschoolers to have an occasional daytime accident. Look for signs of "holding it" and encourage regular potty breaks. Talk to your doctor if your child is not yet potty trained or was previously trained and is now having problems. Sleeping. Preschoolers sleep about 10–13 hours a day. Many 4-year-olds stop taking an afternoon nap, but be sure to schedule some quiet time during the day. 4. Do an exam with your child undressed while you are present. This will include listening to the heart and lungs, observing motor skills, and talking to your child to assess speech and language development. 5. Update vaccines. Vaccines can protect kids from serious childhood illnesses, so it's important that your child get them on time. Vaccine schedules can vary from office to office, so talk to your doctor about what to expect. 6. Order tests. Your doctor may check for anemia, lead, high cholesterol, and tuberculosis and order tests, if needed. How Is My Child Developing at 4 Years? By 4 years, most kids: * say sentences with four or more words * can tell you at least one thing that happened that day * answer simple questions, like “What is a crayon for?” * ask to go play with other children if none are around * comfort others who are hurt or sad * change their behavior based on where they are, like at a library or a playground * draw a person with three or more body parts * can name some colors * can catch a large ball most of the time * unbutton some buttons Talk to your doctor if your child is not meeting one or more milestones, or you notice that your child had skills but has lost them. How Can My 4-Year-Old Stay Healthy? Here are some things to keep in mind until your child's next checkup at 5 years: Eating * Try to eat together as a family most nights of the week. * Serve a variety of healthy foods, including lean meats, fish, fruits, vegetables, and whole grains. * Preschoolers should get 2½ cups (600 ml) of low-fat milk (or other low-fat dairy products, like yogurt) daily. You can also give an unsweetened, fortified soy beverage. * Limit 100% juice to no more than 4–6 ounces (120–180 ml) a day. Safety * Supervise your child outdoors, especially when playing around water and near streets. Consider enrolling your child in a swimming class. * Make sure playground equipment is well maintained and age appropriate. Surfaces should be soft to absorb falls (sand, rubber mats, or a deep layer of wood or rubber chips). * Apply sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher at least 15 minutes before your child goes outside to play and reapply about every two hours. * Protect your child from secondhand smoke, which increases the risk of heart and lung disease. Secondhand vapor from e-cigarettes is also harmful. * Make sure your child always wears a helmet when riding a tricycle or bicycle. * Kids should stay harnessed in a forward-facing car seat in the back seat until they reach the highest weight or height limit. When your child has outgrown this seat, switch to a belt-positioning booster seat until your child is 4 feet 9 inches (150 cm) tall, usually when they're 8–12 years old. * Protect your child from gun injuries by not keeping a gun in the home. If you do have a gun, keep it unloaded and locked away. Ammunition should be locked up separately. Make sure kids can't get to the keys. * Discuss appropriate touch. Teach your child that some body parts are private and no one should see or touch them. Tell your child to come to you if anyone ever asks to look at or touch their private parts, if they're ever asked to look at or touch someone else's private parts, or are asked to keep a secret. * Talk to your doctor if you're concerned about your living situation. A partial note stating “Child is growing well, no concerns” is reassuring, but it is not sufficient as a complete well-child record. The phrase implies that the child’s growth and general development appear normal, but it does not explicitly document the specific measurements, percentiles, or developmental milestones that would support that conclusion. In a 4-year-old, normal growth is expected to include a weight and height that fall within the normal range, a BMI that aligns with the child’s age and sex, and a growth chart plot that shows a consistent upward trajectory without significant deviation from expected percentiles [N3-R1][N3-F2]. Developmentally, a 4-year-old should be meeting age-appropriate milestones in speech, motor skills, social behavior, and emotional regulation, such as saying sentences with four or more words, catching a large ball, drawing a person with three or more body parts, and beginning to name colors [N3-F2]. These are normal findings, but the note does not explicitly state them.

The gaps in the partial note that should be filled explicitly include the actual growth measurements, the plotted growth chart status, and the specific developmental findings. “Growing well” is a general reassurance, but it does not replace recording the child’s weight, height, BMI, and percentile values. It also does not replace documenting whether the child met the 4-year-old developmental milestones or whether there were any red flags such as language delay, motor delay, or social/emotional concerns [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-F2]. The note should also include the provider’s evaluation of the child’s overall health, any concerns raised by the parent, and any clinical judgment about whether further assessment is needed [N2-R1][N2-R5].

When to note reassuring findings versus when to ask for more detail depends on the strength of the partial note. “Growing well, no concerns” is sufficient to indicate that the provider did not identify any immediate red flags, but it is not sufficient to conclude normality without explicit documentation. In a structured note, the provider should explicitly state that growth is normal, the measurements are within expected limits, and the child meets age-appropriate developmental expectations. If the provider is uncertain or if the parent has not provided enough detail, the note should ask for more information rather than assuming normality [N2-R1][N2-R5]. For a 4-year-old, the provider should also consider whether any screening recommendations or developmental surveillance were completed, because “no concerns” does not necessarily mean that all required assessments were done [N5-R1][N5-R3].

A well-child note should include core sections such as history, exam, and plan, with the history covering the subjective concerns and developmental review, the exam covering objective findings, and the plan covering follow-up, anticipatory guidance, and any recommended actions [N1-F1][N6-R3]. The evidence supports a structured SOAP-style note format, where the note is divided into subjective, objective, assessment, and plan, and pediatric notes often include developmental review as part of the overall evaluation [N1-F1][N6-R3]. This means that even a short note should at least contain those elements rather than being reduced to a bare one-sentence conclusion.

Sections that may be omitted or inferred from the partial note are those that are not directly stated in the fragment. The partial note does not include a detailed history, a specific exam, a growth chart record, or a developmental assessment. It also does not include family history, social history, or specific screening results. In the evidence, a well-child note template explicitly includes sections such as parental concerns, physical exam, development, family history, social history, and immunizations, with some of these being checked as normal or documented in detail [N1-F1]. Therefore, a complete note should still include these sections, even if some are inferred as “no concerns” or “normal,” rather than omitting them entirely.

When to include family history, social history, or developmental review depends on the clinical context and the periodicity of the visit. The evidence shows that well-child visits include maternal depression, psychosocial screening, developmental and surveillance assessments, and behavioral/social/emotional screening [N5-R3][N5-R5]. For a 4-year-old, developmental review is particularly important because the note should evaluate the child’s play, speech, learning, movement, and emotional well-being [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-F2]. Family history and social history are also part of the standard note structure and should be included even if the partial note does not provide them, because they help contextualize the child’s health and identify risk factors or protective factors [N1-F1][N6-R2]. In short, the mandatory core sections are history, exam, and plan; optional or inferred sections are those that are not directly stated in the partial note but are still relevant to a complete well-child record [N1-F1][N6-R3].

The evidence supports the idea that providers should keep an adequate stock of vaccines on hand to prevent missed immunizations, and that growth charts are used to track a child’s growth over time [N4-R3][N4-R4]. ## Final structured well-child visit note from the partial note

### 1) Core sections of the note
A well-child visit note should include the core sections of history, exam, assessment, and plan, with the history covering subjective concerns and developmental review, the exam covering objective findings, and the plan covering follow-up and anticipatory guidance [N1-F1][N6-R3]. The evidence also supports including family history, social history, and developmental review as part of the standard well-child record [N1-F1][N6-R2]. In this case, the partial note is too brief to be a complete record, so the structured note must explicitly reconstruct those sections rather than omitting them.

### 2) What should be explicitly documented versus what can be inferred
The phrase “Child is growing well, no concerns” is reassuring, but it does not replace explicit documentation of growth measurements, percentile status, developmental findings, or screening status [N3-R1][N3-F2][N2-R1]. In a 4-year-old, normal growth means the child should have weight, height, BMI, and growth chart values within expected limits, and the child should meet age-appropriate developmental milestones such as speaking in sentences, catching a ball, drawing a person with three or more body parts, and beginning to name colors [N3-F2]. These are normal findings, but they must be explicitly stated in the note.

The partial note also lacks immunization status and growth percentiles, so those should not be assumed or inferred. Instead, the note should either document the current vaccine status or explicitly note that the provider did not review it and that the parent should bring it up next time [N4-R3]. Similarly, the note should either record the plotted growth chart values or explicitly state that growth percentiles were not mentioned and that the provider should review them before concluding normality [N4-R4][N4-R5]. This preserves clinical completeness without overstatement.

### 3) How to handle missing data while preserving clinical completeness
Missing data should be handled by explicitly noting the absence rather than omitting the section. For immunizations, the safest approach is to note the gap and request clarification at the next visit [N4-R3]. For growth percentiles, the note should state that the provider did not document them and that the child’s growth should be reviewed on the growth chart [N4-R4][N4-R5]. For screening recommendations, the absence of results means the note should still document the recommended screenings and note whether they were completed or planned [N5-R1][N5-R3]. If the provider did not complete the screening, the note should state that the screening was discussed, the provider’s concern about missing it, and the plan to complete it [N5-R1][N5-R3].

### 4) Structured sections for a complete note
Below is a structured well-child visit note that turns the partial fragment into a complete record.

---

## **Child: 4-year-old**  
## **Visit type: Well-child exam**

### **1) History**
- **Subjective concerns / parental concerns:**  
  Parent states “Child is growing well, no concerns.”  
  No specific concerns reported about eating, sleeping, toileting, behavior, or development [N3-R2][N3-F2].

- **Developmental review:**  
  The provider should document whether the child met age-appropriate developmental milestones, including speech, motor, social, and emotional development. A 4-year-old should be expected to:  
  - say sentences with four or more words,  
  - tell at least one thing that happened that day,  
  - answer simple questions,  
  - ask to go play with other children,  
  - comfort others who are hurt or sad,  
  - draw a person with three or more body parts,  
  - name some colors,  
  - catch a large ball most of the time,  
  - unbutton some buttons [N3-F2].  
  In this note, those milestones should be explicitly recorded, not assumed from the phrase “growing well.”

- **Family history / social history:**  
  Family history and social history should be included even if not directly stated in the partial note, because they help contextualize the child’s health [N1-F1][N6-R2]. If they are not provided, the note should state that they were not reviewed and ask the parent to provide them at the next visit.

### **2) Exam**
- **General appearance / vital signs:**  
  The provider should document the child’s general appearance and vital signs, ideally including weight, height, BMI, and the plotted growth chart [N3-R1][N3-F2]. The phrase “growing well” is not a substitute for recording the actual measurements and percentile status [N3-F2].

- **Objective findings:**  
  The provider should document the physical exam findings, including:  
  - head/neck,  
  - ears, nose, mouth,  
  - chest, lungs,  
  - abdomen,  
  - skin, musculoskeletal, and neurologic findings [N1-F1][N6-R3].  
  If the provider did not complete the full exam, that should be noted and the incomplete exam should be documented accordingly.

- **Developmental exam:**  
  The provider should note the child’s motor skills, speech/communication, and social/emotional behavior. For a 4-year-old, this should include gross motor skills, fine motor skills, language development, and social behavior [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-F2]. If the provider did not observe these, that should be stated in the note.

### **3) Assessment**
- **Growth and development:**  
  The child appears to be in the normal growth range, but this must be supported by actual measurements, plotted growth chart status, and developmental findings [N3-R1][N3-F2][N2-R1]. If the provider is confident, the note should explicitly state that growth is normal and that developmental milestones are met. If there are gaps, the note should ask for more detail [N2-R1][N2-R5].

- **Immunizations:**  
  Immunization status was not mentioned, so the provider should not assume up-to-date status. The note should either document the current vaccine status or explicitly state that the provider did not review it and that the parent should bring it up next time [N4-R3].

- **Growth percentiles:**  
  Growth percentiles were not mentioned, so the note should either record the plotted growth chart values or explicitly state that growth percentiles were not mentioned and that the provider should review them before concluding normality [N4-R4][N4-R5].

- **Screening recommendations:**  
  The provider should document the recommended screenings and whether they were completed. The AAP and Bright Futures periodicity schedule recommend screenings and assessments at each well-child visit, including growth and development, behavioral/social/emotional screening, and other preventive care elements [N7-R1][N7-R3][N5-R1]. In the absence of results, the note should record the provider’s plan to complete the screening, the provider’s concern about missing it, and any discussion with the parent about when it will be done [N5-R1][N5-R3].

### **4) Plan**
- **Follow-up / next visit:**  
  The provider should schedule the next well-child visit according to the AAP periodicity schedule and note the recommended interval [N7-R1][N7-R3].

- **Anticipatory guidance / counseling:**  
  The provider should give anticipatory guidance on topics such as healthy eating, sleep, safety, and behavior. For a 4-year-old, this should include:  
  - eating habits and healthy snacks,  
  - sleep patterns,  
  - potty training and toileting,  
  - safety around water, playgrounds, and vehicles,  
  - screen time,  
  - readiness for kindergarten, and  
  - prevention of injuries and behavioral concerns [N3-F2][N5-R1][N5-R3].

- **Immunizations / vaccine review:**  
  If immunizations were not reviewed, the provider should schedule a follow-up review and remind the parent to bring the vaccine record next time [N4-R3].

- **Growth review:**  
  If growth percentiles were not discussed, the provider should plan to review the growth chart at the next visit and document the provider’s concern about missing it [N4-R4][N4-R5].

- **Screening completion:**  
  If screening results were not available, the provider should plan to complete the screening and document the provider’s concern about missing it [N5-R1][N5-R3].

### 5) Bottom line
The partial note “Child is growing well, no concerns” is reassuring, but it is not a complete well-child record [N3-F2][N2-R1]. A complete structured note must explicitly document:  
- growth measurements and growth chart status,  
- developmental findings and milestones,  
- immunization status,  
- growth percentiles,  
- screening items, and  
- any gaps or missing data [N3-R1][N3-F2][N4-R3][N4-R4][N5-R1][N5-R3].  

By including these elements, the note preserves clinical completeness while respecting the limits of the partial fragment [N1-F1][N6-R3].

A partial note stating “Child is growing well, no concerns” is reassuring, but it is not sufficient as a complete well-child record. The phrase implies that the child’s growth and general development appear normal, but it does not explicitly document the specific measurements, percentiles, or developmental milestones that would support that conclusion. In a 4-year-old, normal growth is expected to include a weight and height that fall within the normal range, a BMI that aligns with the child’s age and sex, and a growth chart plot that shows a consistent upward trajectory without significant deviation from expected percentiles [N3-R1][N3-F2]. Developmentally, a 4-year-old should be meeting age-appropriate milestones in speech, motor skills, social behavior, and emotional regulation, such as saying sentences with four or more words, catching a large ball, drawing a person with three or more body parts, and beginning to name colors [N3-F2]. These are normal findings, but the note does not explicitly state them.

The gaps in the partial note that should be filled explicitly include the actual growth measurements, the plotted growth chart status, and the specific developmental findings. “Growing well” is a general reassurance, but it does not replace recording the child’s weight, height, BMI, and percentile values. It also does not replace documenting whether the child met the 4-year-old developmental milestones or whether there were any red flags such as language delay, motor delay, or social/emotional concerns [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-F2]. The note should also include the provider’s evaluation of the child’s overall health, any concerns raised by the parent, and any clinical judgment about whether further assessment is needed [N2-R1][N2-R5].

When to note reassuring findings versus when to ask for more detail depends on the strength of the partial note. “Growing well, no concerns” is sufficient to indicate that the provider did not identify any immediate red flags, but it is not sufficient to conclude normality without explicit documentation. In a structured note, the provider should explicitly state that growth is normal, the measurements are within expected limits, and the child meets age-appropriate developmental expectations. If the provider is uncertain or if the parent has not provided enough detail, the note should ask for more information rather than assuming normality [N2-R1][N2-R5]. For a 4-year-old, the provider should also consider whether any screening recommendations or developmental surveillance were completed, because “no concerns” does not necessarily mean that all required assessments were done [N5-R1][N5-R3].

### 1) Core sections of the note
A well-child visit note should include the core sections of history, exam, assessment, and plan, with the history covering subjective concerns and developmental review, the exam covering objective findings, and the plan covering follow-up and anticipatory guidance [N1-F1][N6-R3]. The evidence also supports including family history, social history, and developmental review as part of the standard well-child record [N1-F1][N6-R2]. In this case, the partial note is too brief to be a complete record, so the structured note must explicitly reconstruct those sections rather than omitting them.

### 2) What should be explicitly documented versus what can be inferred
The phrase “Child is growing well, no concerns” is reassuring, but it does not replace explicit documentation of growth measurements, percentile status, developmental findings, or screening status [N3-R1][N3-F2][N2-R1]. In a 4-year-old, normal growth means the child should have weight, height, BMI, and growth chart values within expected limits, and the child should meet age-appropriate developmental milestones such as speaking in sentences, catching a ball, drawing a person with three or more body parts, and beginning to name colors [N3-F2]. These are normal findings, but they must be explicitly stated in the note.

The partial note also lacks immunization status and growth percentiles, so those should not be assumed or inferred. Instead, the note should either document the current vaccine status or explicitly note that the provider did not review it and that the parent should bring it up next time [N4-R3]. Similarly, the note should either record the plotted growth chart values or explicitly state that growth percentiles were not mentioned and that the provider should review them before concluding normality [N4-R4][N4-R5]. This preserves clinical completeness without overstatement.

### 3) How to handle missing data while preserving clinical completeness
Missing data should be handled by explicitly noting the absence rather than omitting the section. For immunizations, the safest approach is to note the gap and request clarification at the next visit [N4-R3]. ## **Visit type: Well-child exam**

- **Subjective concerns / parental concerns:**

  - tell at least one thing that happened that day,  
  - answer simple questions,  
  - ask to go play with other children,  
  - comfort others who are hurt or sad,  
  - draw a person with three or more body parts,  
  - name some colors,  
  - catch a large ball most of the time,  
  - unbutton some buttons [N3-F2].
